items.stem: In a high-context culture, much of a message's meaning is carried by:

options.rationale: That describes a low-context style, where meaning is stated directly.

options.text: Context, relationship and nonverbal cues around the words

Formality of documents is not what high- versus low-context describes.

items.stem: The fairest way to handle recurring meetings for a team split across distant time zones is to:

options.text: Always use the headquarters time zone
options.rationale: This repeatedly burdens the same regions and signals they matter less.

options.text: Rotate inconvenient meeting times so the burden is shared
options.rationale: Correct: rotating the awkward slot spreads the cost of distance across everyone.
Some discussions genuinely need real-time conversation.

options.text: Let the most senior person always pick
options.rationale: Convenience for one person is not the same as fairness for the team.

items.explanation: Correct: rotating the awkward slot spreads the cost of distance across everyone.
items.domain_ref: Working across time zones and distance

items.stem: Which TWO practices help when giving feedback across cultures? (Select TWO)

options.text: Learn whether the person's culture expects direct or indirect feedback
options.rationale: Correct: matching directness to expectation makes feedback usable.

options.text: Protect the person's dignity and avoid public criticism where face matters
options.rationale: Correct: attention to face keeps feedback from causing withdrawal.

options.text: Always deliver feedback as bluntly as possible
options.rationale: Bluntness can destroy trust in cultures that value indirectness and face.

options.text: Assume your own feedback norms are universal
options.rationale: Projecting your norms is the core cross-cultural feedback error.

items.explanation: Correct: matching directness to expectation makes feedback usable.; Correct: attention to face keeps feedback from causing withdrawal.
